entities.name: August Neidhardt von Gneisenau
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
August Wilhelm Antonius Graf Neidhardt von Gneisenau, a towering figure in Prussian military history, was a field marshal whose strategic acumen and radical reforms fundamentally reshaped the Prussian army following its catastrophic defeat at Jena-Auerstedt in 1806. Born in Schildau on October 27, 1760, and dying in Posen on August 23, 1831, Gneisenau, alongside Gerhard von Scharnhorst and Karl von Clausewitz, spearheaded a transformative period that moved the Prussian military from an antiquated, mercenary-based force to a modern, conscripted army capable of challenging Napoleonic dominance. His contributions were crucial to the War of Liberation (1813-1815) and the ultimate defeat of Napoleon at Waterloo.

Gneisenau's early career saw service in the Austrian and British armies before joining Prussia in 1786. His military brilliance became evident during the defense of Kolberg in 1807, one of the few Prussian strongholds to resist French occupation, earning him widespread recognition. Following the Peace of Tilsit, he became a central architect of the Prussian military reforms, advocating for universal conscription, the professionalization of the officer corps, and the creation of a general staff system. He served as Chief of Staff to Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher during the 1813-1815 campaigns, meticulously planning and executing the strategies that led to victories at the Battle of the Katzbach, Leipzig, and particularly the decisive intervention at Waterloo in 1815, where his tactical decisions proved pivotal in turning the tide against Napoleon.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Gneisenau's military reforms and strategic leadership were instrumental in Prussia's recovery from Napoleonic defeat and its subsequent rise as a major European power, culminating in the decisive victory at Waterloo. His work laid the foundation for the professionalization of the Prussian military, influencing global military organization for over a century.
